title: Holes after a pawn push: who covers them?
outcomes: Predicts the new holes a g-pawn push leaves in front of a castled king
Sees when another pawn still guards a square, so the push creates no hole there
Picks the bishop square that covers the holes a push leaves
Checks whether an enemy knight can land on a hole and stay

steps.text: In **Holes: squares your pawns can no longer guard** you found holes already on the board. Now look ahead. A pawn push in front of your castled king makes holes for good, because pawns never move backward. With the e-pawn gone from e7, the push **g6** leaves f6 and h6 unguarded by any pawn. Before you push, list the squares you stop guarding, then ask who could land on them.

steps.caption: Black to move. The g-pawn is still on g7 and the bishop is still on f8.

line.say: The g-pawn passes f6 and h6. No Black pawn can ever guard either square again.
White makes a quiet move. For the moment no Black piece attacks f6.
The bishop arrives on g7 and attacks both holes.

claims.statement: After g6 f6 and h6 are holes in Black's camp.
Right after g6 no Black piece attacks f6.
From g7 the bishop attacks both f6 and h6.

steps.text: A push does not always cost you. If the e-pawn still stands on e7, it guards f6, so g6 leaves only h6. A hole needs a user: it matters when an enemy knight, or a bishop of the right colour, can reach it and stay. *Rule of thumb:* cover the new holes with a bishop or knight before the enemy arrives, or leave the pawn at home.

steps.title: The same hole, one piece different
steps.prompt: In the first two positions the g-pawn has moved and f6 is a hole; only the Black bishop differs (on b7 or on g7). Can the White knight settle on f6? In the third position the e-pawn stands on e7: is f6 a hole at all? Predict, then check.
Think of your own castled position. Which pawn push in front of your king would leave a hole, and which of your pieces could cover it? Write one line.
